props.title: Watership Down

sections.content: Watership Down (1978) revolutionized adult animation by treating its rabbit protagonists with deadly seriousness. Director Martin Rosen adapted Richard Adams' novel into a haunting meditation on survival, faith, and totalitarianism that traumatized a generation of children who mistook it for typical talking-animal fare. The film's unflinching portrayal of violence and death, coupled with Art Garfunkel's haunting "Bright Eyes" soundtrack, created a stark contrast to Disney's sanitized anthropomorphic tales. This pioneering work opened doors for mature animated features like The Plague Dogs (1982) and influenced later dark fantasy animations including The Secret of NIMH (1982).

sections.content: The film's distinctive animation style combines naturalistic animal movement with expressionistic horror elements, particularly in the rabbit mythology sequences featuring the Black Rabbit of Inlé. This visual approach influenced later European animations like The Wolf House (2018) and Fantastic Planet (1973), establishing that animation could tackle complex political metaphors. The warren of Efrafa, ruled by General Woundwort, serves as a clear allegory for fascist states, while the journey of Hazel and Fiver explores leadership, democracy, and community building. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Impact on Adult Animation

Watership Down created a template for serious animated storytelling that resonates in contemporary works like Mary and Max (2009) and Persepolis (2007). Its success proved audiences would accept sophisticated themes in animation, paving the way for studios like Studio Ghibli. The film's environmental messages and critique of human interference with nature prefigured later works like Princess Mononoke (1997), while its unflinching look at death influenced modern adult animations such as Loving Vincent (2017).
